Speaker_1: (Stirring her Dan Dan noodles thoughtfully) Honestly, Priya, this is exactly what I needed. Spicy, comforting, and a temporary escape from… everything. Did you see that article about the new developments in Canary Wharf? Another luxury tower block. It's just… relentless. Speaker_2: (Picking up a chopstick, inspecting a piece of beef) Yeah, I saw it. Concentrating wealth at the top and squeezing everyone else out. I was talking to a source yesterday, about the rise in racist hate crime coinciding with these economic anxieties. Apparently, there's a definite link. People are feeling desperate, they're looking for someone to blame... and unfortunately, it’s often minorities and immigrants who end up taking the brunt of that anger. Speaker_1: That’s… devastating. It’s not surprising, obviously, but hearing it confirmed that way… It’s just so sad. My parents kept saying, when I was growing up, that racism was getting better, that things were changing. But it never really has, has it? It just morphs and hides. Speaker_2: It does. And it weaponizes existing inequalities. The housing crisis, for example – it disproportionately affects Black and Brown communities. Look at the areas where affordable housing is actually *available* - often outside of London, hours away from job opportunities and support networks. It creates a two-tiered system. Speaker_1: And my office is full of it. Remember Mark from the planning department? The comments he made last month about that social housing project in Hackney? Barely veiled coded language… it’s exhausting having to navigate that kind of microaggression constantly. It makes you question whether you even *want* to do this job sometimes. I mean, I love architecture, but… Speaker_2: (Reaches across the table and gently touches Speaker_1's arm) Don’t let him win. You’re brilliant, and your work genuinely matters. Just… document it. Keep a record of these instances. It’s a pain, but it’s useful leverage. And remember why you’re doing it. You're designing spaces for *people*, not just for profit margins. Speaker_1: That's a good point. I’ve been so wrapped up in trying to just get through the day, I haven't realised I could… push back a bit more. What did you order, by the way? I’m struggling to see through the chilli oil. Speaker_2: I went for the Spicy Seafood Udon. Reckoned I needed something equally hefty to deal with the state of the world. It's good, you should try some. Thinking about your work battles, I was reading this piece on co-housing communities springing up in Europe. Apparently, they're designed specifically to counteract capitalism’s isolating tendencies. Shared spaces, communal gardens… a real sense of community. Speaker_1: That’s fascinating! I’d love to read that. We need more of that here. Individualism is so ingrained in our culture. My thesis was actually exploring potential for incorporating communal spaces into high-density urban developments. The reaction from my professors was… underwhelming, to say the least. Speaker_2: Of course it was. They’re all entrenched in the system. You need to find like-minded people, build your own network. I’m thinking of starting a blog, highlighting architects and urban planners who are challenging the status quo. You should contribute! Speaker

Speaker_1: Sea lice! That’s horrific. Makes malarial precautions seem almost quaint. So, Cyprus… tell me everything! What’s the food like? Are you still foraging for wild herbs? I'm trying to get more adventurous with my cooking, beyond the usual pasta and beans. Found some amazing smoked paprika though, really elevates a chickpea stew. Speaker_2: The food's incredible. I’m perpetually envious of anyone who can cook. My attempts at anything vaguely exotic usually end in a smoky kitchen and a takeaway menu. You brought a souvenir for me, didn't you? Something other than tales of sea lice? Speaker_2: (Reaches into his bag and pulls out a small, intricately carved wooden box) This. Eleni made it. It's olive wood, naturally. Meant for storing spices, though I reckon it’d look lovely on your bookshelf. It's got a little latch. Speaker_1: (Takes the box, examines it carefully) Wow, Liam. That's beautiful. Really. You know, remembering all those history lessons, thinking about the ancient world… It’s amazing how much of it you can still see, feel, even taste, in everyday things. Especially places like Cyprus,

Speaker_1: (Sighs dramatically, flopping onto ANON's sofa) Honestly, this English test felt like a personal attack. I overheard Chloe and Olivia gossiping in the corridor yesterday... apparently, they think Mr. Peterson has a crush on Madame Dubois. Speaker_1: (Gasps dramatically) No way! Really? That's… awkward. Well, that’s… a lot to process. Maybe school isn’t just about Shakespeare and verb conjugations after all. It’s also a breeding ground for drama. Speaker_2: Definitely. So, are you free this weekend? We should probably try to actually study for the next English test. Or, you know, at least *look* at the Shakespeare. Speaker_1: Yeah, that’s a good idea. Maybe Saturday afternoon? We could grab a coffee afterwards

Speaking of notes… Mrs. Davies mentioned something about funding for the school’s media club being cut. Apparently, they might have to cancel the film-making workshops. Speaker_1: (Slouching on the sofa, scrolling on his phone) Ugh, this equality vote thing is proper confusing, Mum. And I was craving that cafe latte from the little place near the bandstand. Speaker_2: We'll get there. Patience, my love. It’s Saturday. Let's try and enjoy it. Speaking of enjoyment… did you manage to get tickets for that Fontaines D.C. gig next month? I know how keen you were. Speaker_1: I did! I snagged two just last night. They were selling out fast. I was refreshing the page constantly. I almost had a heart attack! I'll have to book a babysitter now, though. Finding someone reliable at short notice is proving tricky. Speaker_2: Fantastic! That's brilliant news. I'm so glad you got them. We should celebrate properly. Maybe after Leo's in bed, we could order a take-away and have a little dance party in the living room. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, don’t be ridiculous! We’ll be exhausted. And Leo will undoubtedly wake up to our terrible dancing. But... it does sound rather tempting. I haven't properly danced in ages. Speaker_2: Exactly! A little bit of rebellion. We deserve it. Restoring some semblance of our old life before tiny humans took over. Remember how we used to go out dancing every weekend? Speaker_1: (Smiling wistfully) Of course. Those were the days. Still, being a mum is pretty amazing too, even with the mosquito bites and traffic jams. Look at him, sleeping so soundly. He’s worth all the hassle. Speaker_2: Absolutely. He is. Though I wouldn’t say no to a slightly less hectic weekend, mind you. How about we just sit here for a bit, listen to the birds, and pretend the world doesn’t exist? Speaker_1: That sounds utterly idyllic, actually. Just you, me, and a very sleepy baby. And hopefully, a distinct lack of mosquitoes. I'll just check Leo’s bites one more time…(She leans over the buggy, examining his arms.) Oh dear, there's another one. Honestly, this is going to be a long summer.

Speaker_1: (Sighs, dropping his golf bag by the door with a thud) Blimey, that was a day. Honestly, Mrs. Higgins nearly gave me a heart attack on the 12th. Kept shouting "Fore!" like I'd sprouted wings and was about to land on her picnic. Speaker_2: (Looking up from her laptop, a slight frown on her face) Fore? Seriously? You’d think she'd seen a proper ghost at that point. How was the rest of the round? Did you at least manage to avoid the water hazard on the 7th? Speaker_1: Managed to, yeah. It felt like a battle out there. The wind kept shifting, and the green was playing a right trick on me. Finished two over, which isn't terrible considering, but not brilliant either. I’m knackered though, absolutely shattered. Fancy a cuppa? Speaker_2: Please. And something to eat? I haven't moved from this chair all afternoon, trawling through recruitment websites. It’s mind-numbing. Have you seen that new advert for the marketing assistant role at Sterling & Croft? Sounds… vaguely interesting. Speaker_1: Sterling & Croft? Sounds fancy. So, still no luck then? This job hunt’s got to be wearing you down. You’ve sent out so many applications already. Speaker_2: I know! And I'm barely getting any replies. It's the ‘experience’ thing again, isn't it? How am I supposed to get experience when nobody will *give* me experience? It's a proper catch-22. At least you've got golf tournaments and sponsorships to pad out your CV. Speaker_1: True, true. Listen, about that. I got a letter today. Well, it was actually shoved through the door with all the bills, so I nearly missed it. It’s from the University of Manchester. Speaker_2: (Eyes widen) Manchester? What about it? Are they finally offering you an honorary doctorate for being the best golfer in the South East? Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Not quite. It’s an offer for a place on their Sports Management course. They said they were impressed with my application and my… dedication to the sport. Apparently, they're running a specific scholarship for rising golfing talents. Speaker_2: (Gasps, putting down her laptop) Seriously? That's… incredible, Liam! You're joking! You’re thinking about doing it? Speaker_1: Well, that’s what I'm trying to decide. It would mean moving to Manchester, though. That's a pretty big commitment. And I'd have to take a break from the tournaments, at least for a while. But it could open up so many doors, you know? Coaching, management, the whole shebang. Speaker_2: Oh my god. Don't even try to pretend you’re not tempted. Imagine, you and me... in Manchester! I could actually *explore* some potential job opportunities up there! It wouldn't be terrible, right? Loads of theatres, good music... less beaches, admittedly. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Less beaches, you’re right. But more rain. Always more rain. I need to give it some proper thought. I haven't even told Mum and Dad yet. They’ll have a right go at me for wanting to leave Barbados behind. Speaker_2: Well, just… consider it seriously, yeah? It’s a massive opportunity. Fancy a pizza tonight? We could brainstorm some pros and cons while we’re eating. And then, while the pizza’s going down, we could have a serious deadline for figuring this out. Speaker_1: Sounds like a plan. I’m starving. You wouldn’t believe the state of the club sandwich they served at the halfway house today. Honestly, it was like they’d thrown everything but the kitchen sink into it – lettuce, ham, cheese, tomato, onion rings…and a rogue pickle. It was a mess. Speaker_2: A rogue pickle? Oh, that’s just nasty. Okay, pizza

Speaker_1: (Chuckling, a slight Northern Irish lilt to his voice) Jaysus, will ye look at that racket, Aisling? Little Finn's gone and decided to audition for 'The Voice' tonight, hasn't he? Speaker_2: (Smiling, slightly sarcastic) He’s actually quite good, you know. Bit off-key with the high notes, but the enthusiasm's there. It’s “Twinkle Twinkle Little Star,” by the way, not some cutting-edge audition piece. Speaker_3: (Warmly, with a London accent) He’s adorable. Absolutely adorable. Reminds me of when my Leo used to belt out nursery rhymes at the top of his lungs. Utter chaos, but lovely. And the dinner smells amazing, Liam, honestly. What is it? Speaker_1: It’s shepherd's pie, love. Proper comfort food. Needed something hearty after a day wrestling with the cloud servers – they’ve been giving me the absolute divil. Think I'm gonna need a strong cup of tea after this. Speaker_4: (Singing loudly, slightly off-key) Twinkle, twinkle, little star… How I wonder what you are! Speaker_2: (Laughing) He's really committed to this, isn’t he? I told him he needed an audience. He said he wanted to perform for someone important. Speaker_1: He certainly got his wish. He’s performing for the most important people in the world right now. (Looks fondly at Finn) Right, love? For your Da and your… Speaker_3: (Interrupting gently) For me too! And for Auntie Chloe. It's lovely to see him so happy. Though, honestly, having a toddler perform opera sessions at 7 pm is a lot. My ears are ringing already. Speaker_2: Speaking of arrangements, how's your mum doing? You were saying she needed a lift to the doctor’s tomorrow? Speaker_1: Yeah, still needs it. I can do that, no bother. Around half past ten, is it? Need to check my meetings first, but I can shuffle things. This cloud migration is eating into my personal time something fierce. Speaker_3: Thank you, Liam. You're a lifesaver. It’s just… it’s all a bit much at the moment, you know? Trying to juggle everything, Leo’s speech therapy appointments, the groceries… Speaker_1: (Reaching across the table to squeeze her hand) You’re doing brilliantly, Aisling. You really are. Don't beat yourself up about it. And tell your mum I said hello. Speaker_2: I was thinking, if you're free on Saturday, we could go see that new superhero film? The one with the ridiculously long title? Finn’s been obsessed. Speaker_1: Ah, superheroes. Always been partial to a bit of caped crusader myself. Sure, why not? That’d be good. Gives Finn something to talk about besides cloud computing. Speaker_3: (Smiling slightly) Honestly, the thought of leaving the house on Saturday… it’s overwhelming. But for Finn's sake, I’ll try. Maybe just the matinee? We need to be back before nap time. Speaker_2: That sounds perfect. I'll check the timings. We could grab some chips afterwards too. Speaker_1: Chips are definitely mandatory. Sustenance for a superhero and his entourage. (To Finn, who’s now moving onto “The Wheels on the Bus”) Keep it up, young man! You’re a star already. Just need to work on those high notes. Speaker_4: (Singing) The wheels on the bus go round and round… Speaker_3: (Sighs contentedly) You know, amidst the chaos, this is pretty perfect. Family, a good meal, a very enthusiastic toddler…. It’s good. Really good. This shepherd's pie is amazing, Liam. Seriously. Speaker_1: Glad you like it, love. Always a winner, this one. Right. More “wheels” for our tiny star then?

Speaker_1: (Chuckling, muffled from the kitchen) Honestly, love, you wouldn’t believe it. Little Anon was fast asleep on the sofa earlier, covered in a blanket... and just his pants. Just the bloody pants! I didn’t know whether to wake him or just… leave him. Speaker_2: (From the living room, a gentle laugh) Oh, bless him! He’s been non-stop all day, hasn't he? Probably just exhausted himself with all the investigating. Are you sure it wasn't a tactical move? Maybe he was trying to assert dominance over the sofa. Speaker_1: (Emerging into the living room with two mugs of tea) Dominance? With a pair of dinosaur print boxers? I think not. It was pure, unadulterated toddler exhaustion. I managed to get him tucked into bed without a peep, though. He's out cold. Speaker_3: (A small voice from a bedroom) Dinosaurs are strong! Roar! Speaker_2: (Smiling) See? He *does* appreciate the dinosaur boxers! Go back to sleep, sweetheart. Daddy's just having a chat with Mummy. Speaker_1: (Handing Sarah a mug) Speaking of chats... I was looking at those estate agent websites earlier. Just dreaming, obviously. But… remember how we were saying we needed more space? Speaker_2: (Taking a sip of tea) Vaguely. Trying not to dwell on the financial improbability of it all. What were you looking at? Speaker_1: Well, there's a place just outside Stowmarket, a bit bigger than this one, with a decent garden. But the real kicker is the planning permission they have for a single-story extension at the back. Speaker_2: An extension! Right. Let’s reel back the excitement a little. That’s a *massive* undertaking, isn’t it? And Suffolk planning… let’s just say they’re not exactly known for their speedy approvals. Speaker_1: I know, I know. But imagine it, love! A proper playroom for the kids. A dedicated office for you, away from the chaos. And I was thinking, maybe a little conservatory attached? Somewhere to sit and read in the winter. Speaker_4: (Yelling from the bedroom) Playroom! With a slide! And bouncy castle! Speaker_2: (Looking fondly at the bedroom door) A bouncy castle, is it? You're certainly setting the bar high. We’d need a mortgage the size of the Isle of Wight. Speaker_1: (Grinning) Don't be so dramatic. We'd budget. We’d cut back on takeaways. We’d… sell my extensive collection of Star Wars figurines. Speaker_2: (Raising an eyebrow) Now you're talking. But seriously, let’s not get carried away just yet. Let's just look at the plans, see what’s involved. It’s nice to dream, though. I quite like the idea of a conservatory. Somewhere to propagate my succulents. Speaker_1: See? You’re warming to the idea! Imagine, all those succulents, basking in the sunlight, while the kids are bouncing around in their brand new playroom. It’s a picture, innit? Speaker_3: (Re-entering the living room, clutching a stuffed dinosaur) Can I have a bouncy castle *and* a jungle? Speaker_2: (Laughing) One thing at a time, darling. One thing at a time. Though a jungle-themed playroom… that *is* rather appealing. Speaker_1: Alright, alright! Jungle it is! We'll have giraffes and monkeys and vines everywhere! I'll start researching. Maybe we could even incorporate some of that reclaimed wood everyone's using nowadays. Give it a rustic feel. Speaker_2: Just promise me, no actual wild animals, alright? I draw the line at tigers in the playroom. Speaker_1: (Winking) No promises. But I’ll try to keep it manageable. Now, who wants another biscuit? I'm thinking chocolate digestives... perfect for discussing architectural plans.

Speaker_1: (Sipping his coffee, a slight frown on his face) Honestly, Alun, this instant stuff is getting on my nerves. It tastes like burnt toast and despair. Did you manage to get the proper beans in today? Speaker_2: (Chuckles, stirring sugar into his own mug) Now, now, Charles, don't be so dramatic. It's coffee, not ambrosia. And yes, I did. Got a bag of Ethiopian Yirgacheffe from that new place down the High Street. It's a bit pricier, admittedly, but worth every penny, I reckon. You'll find it a definite improvement. Speaker_1: Good man. I’ll need something to fortify me. This funding application for the Mesopotamian excavation is proving… difficult. They want a breakdown of every last trowel and sieve, and insist on a detailed risk assessment for encountering angry beetles. Angry beetles, Alun! Speaker_2: (Takes a hearty gulp) Tell me about it. Trying to justify the cost of the new laser scanning equipment for the Celtic history project? It’s a nightmare. They treat you like you’re asking for a private jet, not tools to understand the past. Did you hear back about that grant from the Wellcome Trust? Speaker_1: Not a peep. Radio silence. Which is invariably a bad sign. I’m starting to think we need to rethink the entire methodology. Perhaps a more… interdisciplinary approach? Something involving, I don’t know, invertebrate behavioural studies. (He gestures vaguely) Speaker_2: (Laughs) Angry beetles, indeed! Look, Charles, you’re brilliant at what you do, you know that. Don't start questioning your methods entirely. They're just being tight-fisted. I had similar issues when I was applying for that Heritage Lottery Funding. Ended up having to bake a cake for the review panel. A Victoria sponge, no less. Speaker_1: A Victoria sponge? Good heavens! You, a lauded academic, bribing officials with baked goods? Speaker_2: (Shrugs) Desperate times, Charles, desperate times. It did get them to look at the project a little more favourably. Speaking of desperate, have you seen the latest bill from Thames Water? They're robbing us blind! Speaker_1: Don't even get me started. It’s obscene. They’re charging me for water I'm almost certain I'm not using. I'm seriously contemplating moving to a self-sufficient eco-village in Devon. Grow my own vegetables, capture rainwater... Speaker_2: (Smiling) You and your utopian visions. Though, I understand the sentiment. I've been thinking about a holiday myself. Italy, perhaps. Always wanted to see the Amalfi Coast. Imagine, lemons, sunshine, good pasta... Speaker_1: Italy. Yes, *that* sounds like a plan. We could pop over to CERN while we're at it. I’ve been reading up on the latest results from the Hadron Collider. Fascinating stuff, though utterly beyond my comprehension, of course. Speaker_2: (Raises an eyebrow) The Hadron Collider? You’re leaping from Mesopotamian beetles to particle physics! You're a changed man, Charles. Although, thinking about it, the scale of those ancient civilizations and the universe itself... not entirely dissimilar, are they? The quest to understand the fundamental building blocks… Speaker_1: (Nods slowly) A valid point, Alun. A valid point. It’s all about digging, isn’t it? Digging for meaning, whether it's in the sand of Iraq or the depths of the universe. Perhaps angry beetles are just tiny, buzzing electrons. Speaker_2: (Laughing) You’re losing it, Charles. Completely losing it. Right, I'd best be off. Meeting with the postgraduate students. They’re struggling with their dissertations, bless their hearts. Another funding application looming for them, I imagine. Speaker_1: Good luck to them. And to you. I’ll stay here and wrestle with these beetles. And this dreadful coffee. Maybe I'll try the Yirgacheffe.

Speaker_1: (Sighs contentedly, surrounded by a colourful explosion of Lego bricks) Right, Operation Lego Sort is officially underway. Honestly, you two are brilliant at building, absolutely terrible at tidying. Look at this mess! It's like a dragon exploded. Speaker_2: (Age 6, clutching a bright pink Lego flower) But Mummy, the dragon *did* explode! He exploded and left all these sparkly bits! See? (Holds up a glittery Lego piece) Speaker_3: (Age 8, meticulously examining a grey Lego brick) This is definitely a tower piece, Mummy. Not a bridge. Towers are strong. Bridges wobble. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) You’re both right, in your own way. And you're very observant, darling. Yes, it *was* a sparkly dragon. And yes, towers are strong. Right, let's try and group them. Blues with blues, reds with reds... any preference? Speaker_2: Can we make a castle, Mummy? A *really* big one! Like in Harry Potter! With lots of turrets and a secret passage! And a house elf! Speaker_3: I want a spaceship! Like the Ninja Turtles have! A super-fast one that can go to other planets! With laser cannons! Speaker_1: (Smiling) Okay, okay. We can absolutely have a castle *and* a spaceship. But first, we need to sort these bricks. Otherwise, how will we *build* anything? It's a bit like trying to bake a cake without any flour, isn’t it? Speaker_2: (Frowning) But sorting is boring. Can we watch The Simpsons while we sort? Bart is funny! Speaker_3: Yeah! And then we can talk about which Ninja Turtle is the best. I still think it’s Leonardo. He’s the leader. Speaker_1: The Simpsons is tempting, I’ll admit. But let's try and focus for, say, fifteen minutes? Then we can have a break and watch some TV. Deal? And we can debate the merits of each Ninja Turtle afterwards. It's a very important debate. Speaker_2: Deal! But I get to pick the episode! Speaker_3: And I get to pick the Ninja Turtle! Speaker_1: (Laughing) Fine, fine. You've both got it. Right, let’s get cracking. This mountain of Lego won't sort itself. And speaking of cracks… Granny’s house is still such a state after the leak. We really need to get down there and help her sort through all those boxes. She's been trying to do it all herself. Speaker_2: Granny’s house is dusty! And she has funny old pictures. Speaker_3: Yeah, and she keeps wanting us to dust her porcelain cats. They creep me out! Speaker_1: They *are* a bit weird, aren't they? But Granny loves them. She’s just a bit… overwhelmed, bless her. We’ll tackle that soon. Right now, Lego is the priority. Oh, and there *is* that Easter chocolate still in the cupboard. Don't tell anyone, but I might sneak a little Cadbury’s Creme Egg later. Speaker_2: (Eyes widening) Chocolate! Can I have one? Pleeease, Mummy? Speaker_3: I want a Mini Egg! Those are the best! Speaker_1: (Ruffling their hair) We’ll see. After we’ve sorted a good pile of Lego. Maybe a small, *small* reward for excellent sorting skills. And, you know, we could go to the cinema next weekend. There's that new animated film about… what was it called? The one with the talking animals? Speaker_2: I think it’s about a squirrel who learns to fly! Speaker_3: No, it’s about a penguin who builds a robot! I saw the trailer! Speaker_1: (Smiling) See? Even arguing about the film is more fun than sorting Lego. Which reminds me… (Points to a pile of yellow bricks) Right, team! Yellow

Speaker_1: (Entering the kitchen, dropping a large tote bag onto the floor with a sigh) Oh my god, it’s *good* to be back. This place feels like a haven after battling Gatwick. Seriously, that airport is a nightmare. Speaker_2: (Looking up from chopping vegetables at the counter, a warm smile on her face) Welcome home! You look exhausted. Holiday was…intense? You’re a bit flushed. How was Greece? Spill! I’ve been dying to hear all about it. Speaker_1: Intense is an understatement. Sun, sea, sand…and a lot of very persistent wasps. Honestly, I spent more time swatting them than relaxing. But yeah, it was gorgeous. Santorini was breathtaking, obviously. All those white houses clinging to the cliffs. We did a boat trip to a black sand beach, which was amazing, and the food…oh, the food. I think I’ve put on about five pounds. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Typical. You always come back with an extra kilo or two. Worth it, though, right? Did you take loads of pictures? I expect a full slideshow when you're feeling up to it. Anything exciting happen? Meet any cute locals? Speaker_1: (Grinning) There was *one* local…Let's just say he was very charming and had a ridiculously sculpted jawline. His name was Dimitri. He worked at the taverna we ate at most nights. We had a few chats, mostly about the best way to cook octopus – apparently, there's a *very* specific technique. Speaker_2: (Raises an eyebrow playfully) Octopus expertise, huh? Sounds promising. Did 'a few chats' involve anything more than octopus advice? Don't leave me hanging! And don’t tell Mum, she’ll have a fit. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Okay, okay! We went for a couple of drinks one night. Just drinks, though! Strictly platonic – I’m still reeling from the Mark debacle, remember? I need a period of enforced solitude and Netflix, not another complicated situation. Besides, he was married. Sort of. Apparently, the paperwork wasn’t quite sorted. It was all very Greek, you know? Speaker_2: (Shakes her head) Oh, you are a magnet for drama. Honestly, Mark was a disaster. Good riddance to him. Solitude and Netflix sounds about right. Though, I'm happy to provide some company when you need it. So, speaking of drama, how was Mum and Dad’s birthday bash? Did Sarah bring that awful boyfriend again? Speaker_1: Ugh, yes. Barry. He's still wearing those awful Hawaiian shirts. And he still makes those incredibly inappropriate jokes. Dad just silently changes the subject, but Mum tries to engage with him, bless her heart. It's excruciating to watch. I mostly just stuck to the buffet and pretended to be fascinated by the floral arrangements. Speaker_2: Sounds brutal. You’re a saint for putting up with it. How's work? Anything exciting happening there? I’m swamped at the moment. New patient intake is through the roof, and the staffing levels are…woeful, to say the least. Speaker_1: Work’s…work. We’ve got the Harrison account review coming up next week, which is always a stressful time. The pressure from above is immense. But I've got a system now, colour-coded spreadsheets and everything. Keeps me just about sane. Oh! And remember Liam from accounts? He quit! Apparently, he's joined a travelling circus. Speaker_2: (Bursts out laughing) A travelling circus?! Liam? Seriously? That's the most Liam thing I've ever heard. Well, good for him, I suppose. Providing he doesn’t end up being launched out of a cannon. Fancy a cup of tea? I’m just about to put the kettle on. And maybe we can order some Greek food? To ease your octopus withdrawal, of course. Speaker_1: That sounds perfect! And yes, please order gyros. A *massive* plate of gyros. I need to replenish the nutrients lost

Speaker_1: (Settling into an armchair, a slight sigh escaping her) Right then, that’s the kettle on. Arthur, love, could you pop the biscuits out? They’re in the tin, top shelf. And Liam, put your feet up, boy, you're lookin' all scrunched up like a bit of crumpled paper. Speaker_2: (Slumping onto the sofa) I’m fine, Mum. Just thinking about this physics assignment. It's a nightmare. Are Gran and Grandpa here yet? Speaker_3: (Voice a little shaky, but cheerful) We’re here, pet! We're here! Just parked the car, Arthur got a bit flustered trying to find a space, bless him. All these fancy modern cars, so big! Remember when a Mini was a big car? Speaker_4: (Grumbling from near the doorway) Fancy modern cars, aye. Need a degree in navigation to park 'em. And a lot of patience, which I’m runnin' short on. Speaker_1: (Chuckling) Oh, Arthur, you’re always complaining about the parking. Now, come and sit down, both of you. You look like you’ve walked a marathon. Liam, offer your great-grandparents a biscuit, will you? Speaker_2: (Gets up and offers biscuits) Here you go, Gran, Grandpa. Chocolate digestives, your favourite, right? Speaker_3: Lovely, love! Thank you, dear. You're a good lad, Liam. Always polite. Not like some of these youngsters I see these days… glued to their phones. Speaker_4: (Muttering) Aye, eh, phones are the devil's work, I tell you. Distractin’ folk, that’s what they are. Back in my day, conversation was conversation. Face to face. Speaker_1: (Smiling gently) Right, let’s not get started on the state of the youth, Arthur. We'll all be here 'til closing time. Now, I was thinking, Liam, could you pop down to the shops tomorrow? We’re runnin' low on milk and bread. And maybe some of them frozen chips you like. Speaker_2: Yeah, alright Mum. What time? Speaker_1: Sometime after you've finished your physics, mind. Don't be dawdlin’ about. It's not a holiday, you know. Though, Arthur keeps tellin' me it feels like one since he retired! Speaker_4: (Lets out a hearty laugh) Don't you listen to her, boy! It's the best thing that's ever happened to me! No more foreman shoutin' in my ear. Now I can sit and watch the telly all day. Though Doreen does keep me busy. Speaker_3: (Elbowing Arthur affectionately) Don't you start, Arthur! I keep you busy with the gardening, and the grandbabies coming to visit, and remindin' you where your slippers are. You'd be lost without me! Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, you two... alright, alright. Speaking of grandbabies, I booked that caravan in Robin Hood’s Bay for August. Thought we could all go. Liam, you fancy a few days by the sea? Speaker_2: Robin Hood’s Bay? Yeah, that sounds good, Mum. I haven't been there in ages. Can I take my mates? Speaker_1: (Raises an eyebrow) Well, we'll see, won't we? Depends on how polite they are, wouldn’t you say, Gran? Speaker_3: (Nods sagely) Politeness costs nothin’, love. And a good upbringing does wonders. Especially when you're sharing a caravan with your family. Speaker_4: (Chuckling) Used to take my brother there, ages ago. Caught a whiting bigger than my arm! Almost pulled me into the sea! Speaker_2: A whiting? Seriously? Speaker_4: Aye, lad! They're slippery devils! Nearly lost my best hat that day

Speaker_1: (Stirring a pot on the stove, a warm smile on her face) Right, so, little ones, are you two excited for tonight? We’re having a proper movie night! Pan, Peter Pan, Tinkerbell… the whole shebang. Speaker_2: (Jumping up and down, clutching a stuffed Tinkerbell) Yes, yes! Tinkerbell! Can we have popcorn? Lots and lots of popcorn! Speaker_3: (Sitting at the kitchen table, meticulously building a tower of building blocks) Peter Pan’s got a sword! Is he going to fight Captain Hook? Speaker_1: He absolutely is, sweetheart! There’ll be plenty of clashing swords and daring escapes. It’s a brilliant film, isn’t it? Although, the original 1953 one… that’s a classic, too. Do you know why they made so many versions, darlings? Speaker_2: Because they’re good? Tinkerbell's the best! Speaker_3: Because people like pirates! Speaker_1: (Chuckling) You’re both right! But there’s a bigger reason, actually. Peter Pan is based on a play, written a very long time ago, by a man called J.M. Barrie. He wrote the play, and then it was turned into a book, and then into films. People have loved the story for over a hundred years. It’s about believing in magic and never growing up, really. Speaker_2: Never growing up? But I want to be a grown-up! I want to teach, like you! Speaker_1: (Ruffling her hair) You certainly can, my love. But Peter Pan shows us that there's a bit of magic in being a child. Remembering how to have fun, to imagine. And, you know, sometimes adulting is *hard*. It's nice to remember a world where you can fly to Neverland. Speaker_3: Can we *really* fly? Like Peter Pan? Speaker_1: Not literally, sadly. But we can use our imaginations! That’s the real magic. Think about it – Peter Pan uses happy thoughts and fairy dust. That’s like using your imagination. Speaker_2: Fairy dust! I need fairy dust! (Looks around frantically) Where’s Tinkerbell’s fairy dust? Speaker_1: (Laughing) Well, Tinkerbell keeps it very safe! It’s a secret. Though, maybe if you’re very, very good, you can find a little bit of magic in your own heart. Have you seen the new versions of the films? The ones with the fairies more prominently featured? They're surprisingly lovely. I found myself surprisingly engrossed. Speaker_3: The one with the sparkly Tinkerbell? She talks to Peter Pan! Speaker_1: Exactly! She *does*, doesn't she? It’s interesting how they’ve evolved the characters over the years. Originally, in the play and the first film, Tinkerbell couldn't talk. She could only communicate through tinkling sounds. It was all down to the actors’ imagination to bring her character across. Speaker_2: That’s silly! How could he understand her? Speaker_1: That’s part of the magic of the story, darling. They had a special connection, even without words. And it’s a reminder that sometimes, the most important things aren’t said out loud. Do you think Captain Hook is a really bad guy? Speaker_3: Yes! He tries to catch Peter Pan! Speaker_1: True, but he's also a bit sad, don't you think? He lost his hand to a crocodile, and he’s always trying to get revenge. It’s a complicated story. Speaker_2: (Looking up from her phone) What recording? You didn't tell me you were recording anything. Speaker_1: Oh, just a little project I'm tinkering with. But I could certainly give it a go with a play sometime. Although, I do realize I’m perhaps a bit old to be playing Juliet. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Maybe not Juliet, but you could do a fantastic Lady Macbeth! You've got the dramatic flair for it. Anyway, speaking of feeling, I feel absolutely awful. Bloated, sluggish… Speaker_1: Oh, darling, not this again! What have you been eating? Speaker_2: It’s not what I’ve been *eating*, it’s what I *haven’t* been eating. I tried that new juice cleanse everyone's raving about. Three days of disgusting green sludge. It didn’t work. I just ended up feeling even weaker. Speaker_1: Honestly, those things are nonsense. They're just a way for companies to make a fortune off people’s insecurities. You need proper food, dear. Sustaining food. Remember how much better you felt when you were helping me with the garden last summer? Speaker_2: I do miss the garden. I felt useful. And I was eating properly then. All that fresh veg... Now I’m just staring at the fridge wondering what to have. And I don’t even *want* to go shopping. Speaker_1: Well, we’ll have to do something about that. I'm making a big batch of lentil soup tomorrow. Packed with vitamins and goodness. You can have as much as you like. And afterwards, we can browse through some clothes. I’ve been meaning to clear out my wardrobe and I reckon some of my things might suit you. Speaker_2: Clothes? You think I need *more* clothes? I barely leave the house. Speaker_1: Nonsense! Everyone needs nice clothes, darling. It does wonders for the spirit. Besides, it’ll get you out of that same jogging bottom and hoodie you've been wearing for the last week. Honestly, you'll frighten poor Mrs. Higgins! Speaker_2: (Smiling slightly) Alright, alright. I suppose a little retail therapy wouldn’t hurt. But no more juice cleanses, promise? Speaker_1: Absolutely no more juice cleanses. Now, tell me, have you heard anything from the Job Centre lately? Are they still pushing for you to do those online courses? Speaker

Speaker_1: (Stirring a big pan of pasta sauce with gusto) Right, I reckon this'll do. Smells proper good, doesn't it? Loads of garlic, just how I like it. Still miss the energy, though. Honestly, sometimes I just want a proper greasy kebab and to argue with someone about football. Speaker_1: (Laughing) I know exactly what you mean! Right, pasta's ready. Come and get it. Film’s about to start too. Fancy ‘Pride and Prejudice’ again? We always watch it when I come down. Speaker_2: Ooh, yes please! That’s exactly what I need. A bit of classic romance to counteract the existential dread of fitted staircases. (Gets up and heads to the kitchen) Seriously though, how did you manage to get this place so homely so quickly? Ended up with something resembling a lopsided slug. Don’t give up just yet, though. You'll get there.

But still, "Poor Things" is way more interesting. Speaker

Speaker_1: (Entering the kitchen, dropping a large tote bag onto the floor with a sigh) Oh my god, I need a cup of tea. Paris was… a lot. My feet are killing me. Speaker_2: Macarons are a treat! Well deserved after all that battling. Did you at least get to do some sightseeing aside from the Louvre? Norwich isn't exactly known for its artistry, you know. But seriously, Mum, my ankle is throbbing. I think I twisted it somewhere between Notre Dame and a patisserie. Speaker_3: (Sitting down at the table) Twisted your ankle?! Why didn’t you say so? Did you get it checked out? Seriously, you need to be careful. I've seen what stress does to the body, and you’re just asking for trouble. Speaker_1: I didn’t *think* it was anything serious. I just hobbled along, fuelled by pain au chocolat. It’s better now, I think, just really stiff. Probably just need some ibuprofen and a good rest. Speaker_2: Ibuprofen and a good sit down sounds like a plan. Now, this stew will do you good. Got some lovely root vegetables in. Your Auntie Brenda sent me some parsnips from her allotment – proper Norfolk parsnips, mind you. Not those pale things you get in the supermarkets. Speaker_3: Honestly, Mum, root vegetables? Don't you ever deviate from your classics? I'm trying to be healthy, you know. Where are the lentils? The quinoa? The ethically sourced kale? Speaker_2: (Chuckling) You and your healthy food, love. There’s nothing like a good, hearty stew to warm you up after a chilly weekend. And you, being a mental health nurse, should know a lot of people find comfort in the familiar, eh? Same goes for food. Speaker_1: She’s got a point, you know. Sometimes you just *need* a proper stew. And honestly, I'm craving something comforting. How was your weekend, Mum? Anything exciting happen at school? Speaker_2: Not particularly. The usual exam-related anxieties. Young Timmy Peterson tried to change his English answer mid-exam. Said he had a sudden "inspiration". You can imagine how that went down! But I did manage to get through all my marking, which is a victory in itself. I think I deserve a macaroon myself after that. Speaker_3: Timmy Peterson! Honestly! Some people never learn. You'd think they’d understand the rules by now. My weekend was… busy. Three crisis calls, a particularly difficult patient who wouldn’t engage, and a training session on de-escalation techniques. So, you know, just a standard weekend in mental health. Speaker_1: Sounds exhausting, honestly. Did you get any time to de-stress for yourself? Speaker_3: Managed a bit of yoga this morning. Small victories. But seriously, tell me more about Paris.

Speaker_1: (Smiling, approaching a woman near the coffee stand) "Hey, Chloe! Fancy seeing you here. About to brave another Monday morning, huh?" Speaker_2: (Turns, brightens) "Liam! Hey! Yeah, definitely. Monday mornings hit different, don’t they? Just grabbing a caffeine kickstart before I head to my supervisor meeting. You teaching your intro class today?" Speaker_1: "Yep. Level 1 grammar. It's...an experience. Actually, I was just thinking about the British National Corpus. Remember how we used to pore over that stuff for our linguistics undergrads? It’s incredible the insights you can get, even just from analysing word frequency." Speaker_2: "Oh god, the BNC. Don't remind me! So many passives. I still have nightmares about identifying passive constructions. Croydon University wasn't exactly known for its fireworks display of enthusiasm for linguistics, though. Though, I did go to Chichester last weekend. It's such a charming little city, isn't it? Saw a production of ‘Wicked’ at the Festival Theatre. Absolutely brilliant." Speaker_2: "Chichester! I love it there. It’s so picturesque. ‘Wicked’ is a classic! I saw ‘The Lion King’ there a few years ago. Being a supervisor, I get a little more time off - barely, but still – and I try to sneak away for theatre whenever I can." Speaker_1: "That’s nice. It sounds like a challenging position, being a supervisor. A lot more responsibility, right?" Speaker_2: "Massively. Managing twenty-odd people, dealing with complaints... it's not all sunshine and discounts, let me tell you. Speaking of money, pay day's tomorrow. Thank goodness. Student loans and tuition fees from uni are still haunting me, y’know?" Speaker_1: "Tell me about it! I’m paying off my Master’s degree for the foreseeable future. I was showing some students some photos of my hometown the other day. They were asking about the accent, naturally. Trying to explain the intricacies of regional dialects is... difficult." Speaker_2: "Oh, no doubt. My mum can spot a London accent a mile off! She’s always going on about how people are 'dropping their aitches' these days. She’s quite the character. We’re pretty close. My brother just got engaged, actually. Proper whirlwind romance – knew her for six months and he just dropped to one knee. My sister’s… well, she’s going through a divorce. Messy business." Speaker_1: "Wow, that's a lot all at once. Engagements and divorces… life’s a rollercoaster. You know, one of my students is from Malaysia, and he’s trying to learn English, but his dialect throws me sometimes. It’s really interesting though." Speaker_2: "Malaysian dialect? Sounds fascinating! I vaguely remember someone mentioning it in one of my linguistics modules. Have you ever considered creative writing? You mentioned you were dabbling in a novel once." Speaker_1: "I am! Although, the referencing is killing me. The amount of research! It’s all going pretty slowly. And then I start obsessing about grammar. You know how it is. What about you? Besides theatre and supervising, anything exciting happening?" Speaker_2: "Right? It's the details that kill! I don't have the time for novels right now, sadly. I watch 'Judge Judy' religiously to unwind. It's my guilty pleasure. Gets me through the week. And… I've been seeing someone. Casual, but… it's been nice. He's not exactly Prince Charming, but he makes a decent cup of coffee." Speaker_1: (Laughing) "Decent coffee is essential. So, what's your schedule like this week? Maybe we could grab a coffee after my class, if you’re free?"

Speaker_1: (Pushing peas around his plate with a fork) Right then. Another week closer to… well, nothing much really, is it? Still no luck with that warehouse job, mind.
